papers.title: Hypothesis Generation and Semantic Attribution in Inverse Perturbation Modeling
papers.summary: Understanding gene regulatory relationships at scale can help identify intervention points and anticipate unintended effects, but connecting a black-box model's learned computation to biological knowledge remains difficult. We investigate whether a sparse, typed gene network can generate inspectable hypotheses for steering malignant transcriptional programs toward expression patterns associated with favorable prognosis. Using LINCS L1000 CRISPR/Cas9 profiles paired with matched plate controls, we train a graph neural network to recover the perturbed gene from baseline and endpoint expression. Nodes combine ProTrek-derived protein representations with expression features; edges encode signed regulatory relationships and other gene interactions. We use this inverse formulation to nominate interventions for a desired multigene expression change in a specified cancer-cell context, and use integrated gradients and conductance along a path from the cell baseline toward the requested endpoint to attribute each nomination to gene states, typed messages, and residual connections. In A549, the model nominates TTK although its expression is unchanged in the request; the account assigns supporting credit through the checkpoint-associated MAD1L1 relationship and opposing credit through the E2F4 transcriptional-regulatory channel. Across 333 screened nominations in nine held-out cell lines, request-path attribution shows positive line-averaged correspondence with finite message-deletion effects at every transition. Existing TTK knockout measurements show requested-direction agreement across other markers at the 98.2nd percentile (10 wells), and ten of seventeen measured cases in the illustrative screen meet the predefined support criterion. These analyses make competing biological accounts of a nomination examinable and open to experimental test.

papers.title: Certified Comparative Statics for Conservation-Law Equilibrium Layers, with an Application to RNA Interference
papers.summary: Implicit and equilibrium neural layers define their output as the fixed point of a map. Existing theory certifies that this fixed point exists; it does not certify how it responds to its inputs. For a conservation-law layer with order-preserving coupling we give a form-independent answer: every input-output comparative static is sign-certified if and only if the residual Jacobian is a nonsingular M-matrix, and the certified sign depends only on the sign of the occupancy derivative, so one guarantee covers Langmuir, Hill, and saturating-exponential occupancies. The M-matrix machinery is classical; the contribution is form-independence as the portable invariant, the first certified-sign sensitivity result for a layer of this class, and a sharp phase boundary at which certification is lost while the equilibrium remains well posed. Three consequences follow: the phase boundary, which is strictly stronger than the M-matrix condition; competitive derepression, whose derivative is identically zero for any independent per-target scorer and provably nonzero here; and non-submodularity of resource-coupled suppression. We instantiate on siRNA off-target competition and validate on real public data only, across seventeen microRNAs, two titration studies, and a paired chemical-modification experiment; a second, non-biological instantiation shows the same certified sign on measured physical data. As a trainable layer the operator learns end-to-end while remaining certified-monotone by construction, reaching magnitude parity with a parameter-matched feedforward baseline while expressing a competition effect that baseline cannot represent for any weights. The single-pool instantiation validates the mechanism but does not rank off-target magnitude or resolve position-specific design. Code: https://github.com/shadi97kh/certified-equilibrium-layers

papers.title: Mirror Descent at the Edge of Stability
papers.summary: In many deep learning settings, gradient descent has been shown to operate at the edge of stability -- a regime where the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian hovers around $2/η$. We study this phenomenon in mirror descent, a generalization of gradient descent. As mirror descent is non-Euclidean, existing explanations of the edge of stability phase do not extend to this setting. We generalize the existing notion of sharpness to introduce mirror sharpness, which measures the curvature of the loss with respect to the mirror potential. Empirically, we observe that the mirror sharpness hovers slightly above the $2/η$ threshold. Furthermore, we derive a dual central flow ODE for mirror descent that models iterates in continuous time at the onset of edge of stability. Our ODE provides insights into the difficulties of extending existing arguments for why sharpness stabilizes at $2/η$ from gradient descent to mirror descent in full generality.

papers.title: A Finite-Rate Selection Law for Annealed Gibbs Sampling
papers.summary: Annealed Gibbs sampling samples a multimodal model by redrawing one variable at a time from its conditional distribution as the temperature falls from a high value, where the distribution is broad, to the target temperature. Each run ends in a single mode, and unbiased Monte Carlo estimates require the runs to end in each mode in proportion to its probability under the model. At a finite cooling rate this can fail. We measure the error by $c$, the fraction of the model's log-odds between two modes that the samples retain. In the Curie--Weiss model, where a weak external field favors one of two modes, each run selects its mode near the transition at which the modes form, and rarely switches once they have separated. Near the transition, the random fluctuations of the Gibbs updates still outweigh the weak field, which therefore biases the choice of mode only slightly. Building on the selection probability of Kondepudi and coworkers, we derive a law for $c$ that agrees with an exact computation to within $2\%$ on nine linear cooling ramps. For the Hopfield model, whose modes are stored patterns and their negatives, we derive a factor by which competition among patterns raises $c$. The $c$ measured over random pattern sets lies within $3$--$6\%$ of its prediction, but single pattern sets depart from it, contrary to its derivation.

papers.title: Do Larger Fully Connected Neural Networks Generalize Better?
papers.summary: Greater neural-network capacity does not necessarily yield better performance on unseen data. This study investigates whether a deeper, fully connected neural-network architecture generalizes better than a shallower architecture on the Fashion-MNIST dataset. We compare two architectures under two learning rates and two L2-regularization settings, producing eight configurations. The architectures contain 95,410 and 561,470 trainable parameters, respectively, an approximately 5.9-fold difference. Checkpoints and the final configuration are selected by validation loss, and all configurations are evaluated on a held-out test set. The selected larger configuration achieves 89.82% validation accuracy and 88.77% test accuracy. Selecting the lowest-validation-loss configuration within each architecture yields test accuracies of 88.77% and 88.52%, respectively, a difference of 0.25 percentage points. Across matched training settings, the larger architecture achieves higher test accuracy in only one of four comparisons. Class-level errors are concentrated among visually similar garment categories, and qualitative pixel-removal analyses suggest sensitivity to shape and boundaries. Overall, the findings suggest that increasing architectural capacity alone does not guarantee better generalization, highlighting the importance of considering optimization and regularization when selecting neural-network architectures.

papers.title: Mirrored Min-of-K Training
papers.summary: Min-of-K (MoK) training is widely used to train models that produce diverse outputs from random noise. For each target, it draws K outputs from the model and backpropagates only through the one closest to the target. However, MoK generally does not make the generated distribution match the data distribution. In this paper, we analyze the MoK bias across all values of K and show that tuning K shifts between failure modes, from mode dropping at small K to distribution flattening at large K. We further prove that every nontrivial loss based only on target-candidate distances fails to recover some data distribution, since these distances do not reveal how the candidates are placed relative to each other. Based on these analyses, we propose mirrored MoK (MMoK), a drop-in modification of MoK training that draws one extra sample from the model, applies the closest-candidate selection rule against it, and subtracts the resulting distance. Since this distance is measured between samples of the model, it provides additional information about how the candidates are placed relative to each other. We prove that MMoK can in principle recover data distributions that MoK cannot. We empirically validate MMoK on five scenarios, namely synthetic mixtures, pedestrian and vehicle trajectory prediction, tropical cyclone forecasting, robotic policy learning, and ambiguous medical image segmentation. The results confirm the effectiveness and generality of MMoK in both distribution learning and task performance.

papers.title: Demystifying Classifier-Free Guidance for Auto-Regressive Image Generation
papers.summary: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) has been widely adopted in autoregressive (AR) models for high-quality image generation. Despite its strong empirical performance, its mechanism in AR models remains unclear. This paper demystifies the mechanism of CFG through both empirical and theoretical studies. By examining the top-ranked semantics of different components in CFG, we show that texture information is primarily encoded in the difference between the conditional and unconditional logits, whereas both logits share previous-token repetition as their leading semantics. This strong repetition semantics obscures the desired texture information, causing greedy decoding from the conditional logits alone to produce nearly pure-color images. Through a training-dynamics analysis of shallow transformers, we prove that this shared repetition semantics does not arise from limitations or failures of pretraining, but instead originates from the texture sparsity of images. We further show that CFG improves generation quality by rectifying this repetition bias during inference. Motivated by the shared semantics between conditional and unconditional logits, we propose Attention Weight Reuse (AttnReuse), which reuses intermediate attention computations from the conditional-logit forward pass to accelerate the unconditional-logit computation. AttnReuse reduces about $25\%$ of attention computation with little performance degradation across different models.

papers.title: S$^2$LMR: Supervised Sequential Long-Context Multi-Step Retriever
papers.summary: Multi-step retrieval over long contexts is a key capability for retrieval-augmented generation, but strong existing approaches are costly and complex to train. Supervised retrievers are far simpler and cheaper, yet they fall well behind in this setting. We show that this gap stems not from supervised training itself, but from three misalignments between training and inference: easy training negatives, noisy retrieval prefixes, and position-agnostic scoring. Guided by this analysis, we introduce S$^2$LMR, a simple yet effective supervised sequential retriever that models multi-step retrieval as the evolution of an explicit textual state encoded by a single shared Transformer. On long-context reasoning, multi-hop QA, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks with context lengths ranging from 4K to 10M tokens, S$^2$LMR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, substantially outperforming prior supervised retrievers. Notably, it requires only $\sim$2 hours of training on a single A6000 for contexts of up to 10M tokens, while remaining robust across a wide range of hyperparameter settings.

papers.title: CLASP: Complementary Layer Selection and Profiling for Zero-Shot OOD Detection using Vision-Language Models
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in medical imaging, yet existing approaches often rely on final-layer confidence or entropy-based layer selection, potentially missing complementary information. We show that low in-distribution (ID) confidence entropy does not reliably predict OOD discrimination. We introduce CLASP (Complementary Layer Selection and Profiling), an ID-only framework that jointly models layer--prompt responses and visual features. CLASP ranks visual encoder layers using Gaussian conditional mutual information and selects a compact subset through anchored spectral selection, without fixing the number of layers. It then combines the selected layer--prompt profiles with PCA-compressed visual embeddings and fits a single shrinkage-regularized Gaussian. OOD scores are computed using squared Mahalanobis distance, without fine-tuning, OOD training data, or test-time adaptation. Across histopathology, chest X-ray, and brain MRI benchmarks with UniMedCLIP and BioMedCLIP, CLASP performs strongly under varied distribution shifts. On MIDOG near-OOD, it achieves 87.54% AUROC with UniMedCLIP, outperforming confidence-based baselines; with BioMedCLIP, it remains competitive but trails visual-only Mahalanobis modeling. Ablations highlight the value of layer--prompt interactions and cross-feature dependencies, while exposing shift-dependent contributions and limitations under semantic shifts.

papers.title: Stochastic non-metric MDS for noisy high-dimensional data
papers.summary: Multidimensional scaling (MDS) constructs low-dimensional embeddings that approximate pairwise distances in a high-dimensional dataset. MDS exists in several flavors, with metric MDS approximating distances directly and non-metric MDS additionally optimizing for an arbitrary monotonic transformation of the high-dimensional distances. Empirically, metric MDS is known to suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Here we extend prior theoretical results for metric MDS on fully uninformative data to a more general case of finite, high-dimensional data with concentrated distances. We show that the metric MDS embeddings of such datasets stay distributionally close to the data-independent limit case. We then show that non-metric MDS is more robust to high-dimensional noise and can yield informative embeddings of such data. While existing implementations of non-metric MDS are slow, we develop a fast implementation using stochastic gradient descent in PyTorch. Using our implementation, we conduct an empirical study using multiple simulated and real-world datasets, including population-genomic and scRNA-seq data, and show that non-metric MDS can strongly outperform other methods in terms of global structure preservation.

papers.title: Global Stability and Loss Convergence in Matrix Factorization
papers.summary: We study the matrix factorization objective $\mathcal L(X,Y)=f(XY)$ for convex, twice continuously differentiable output losses with bounded and Lipschitz gradient and a minimizing set that is compact modulo specified input and output invariances. This includes the well-known cross entropy loss. We prove that a positive learning-rate threshold guarantees bounded parameters, summability of squared gradients, and convergence of the loss from every finite initialization. The proof constructs a quantity from the imbalance between parameter matrices that decreases over every step of the gradient descent trajectory.

papers.title: Learning from Another Angle: Rotation-Based Test-Time Training for Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on vision-language tasks but often remain vulnerable to distribution shifts due to their fixed parameters during inference. While Test-Time Training (TTT) offers a pathway for dynamic adaptation, existing approaches suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to multiple sampling and the risk of error reinforcement from biased self-generated supervision. In light of this view, we propose RoTTT (Rotation-based Test-Time Training), a simple and efficient TTT approach that enables instance-specific refinement at inference time. For each test instance, RoTTT performs a small number of gradient updates by predicting the rotation angle of the input image. The known rotation angles naturally serve as a reliable self-supervised signal, enabling lightweight and stable adaptation without requiring additional annotations. Extensive experiments across multiple vision-language benchmarks demonstrate that RoTTT consistently improves performance across different MLLMs, providing a practical and efficient paradigm for on-the-fly MLLM adaptation.

papers.title: When Wrong Answers Remain Unsettled: Failure Dynamics in Recurrent Reasoners
papers.summary: When a recurrent reasoner returns a wrong answer, is its computation finished or merely stopped? We test this on a trained Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM; 27M parameters, Sudoku-Extreme) by running the recurrence for one more inference budget and comparing with an unperturbed control. Solved answers persist (0.95 of 512 endpoints). Wrong answers mostly do not: 0.42 of near-miss answers (n=170) and 0.18 of all 512 wrong endpoints keep their answer. Perturbations from 0.05x to 20x the terminal-update scale barely change these rates, so the measurement reflects continued recurrence, not noise sensitivity. The solved-above-wrong ordering also holds in five further settings (a second seed, TRM, Maze, GRAM-guided TRM, N-Queens), but a fixed 1/2 persistence threshold does not, and neither do HRM's endpoint-spectrum and fast-versus-slow predictability patterns, which are not universal diagnostics. Perturb-and-reselect (known from prior work) is consistent with this: frozen noise gains 4.8 accuracy points (197 gained, 2 lost), but compute-matched extended depth gains 5.6 and Sudoku symmetry augmentation 34.6, so noise is not the best use of the budget. Conclusions are limited to finite horizons and one primary HRM checkpoint; they do not exclude asymptotic attractors.

papers.title: MolReJev: Decision Models Are In-Context Molecular Predictors
papers.summary: Molecular prediction helps prioritize compounds for screening. Specialized predictors are trained for a fixed set of tasks, limiting cross-task generalization. Language models can condition on task descriptions and have recently shown promise in molecular prediction. However, generating answers token by token adds inference cost, and general-purpose models often lack task-specific molecular knowledge. We thus propose MolReJev, which combines Jev-style candidate scoring with in-context learning (ICL) on a language model. MolReJev retrieves similar labeled examples from existing task data and scores candidate labels jointly in one forward pass. ICL improves predictions from the released general-purpose Kev checkpoint and the separately trained MolReJev. For the trained model, gains span all evaluation groups, including held-out tasks, and extend to compounds absent from training. MolReJev generally outperforms MolecularGPT on matched evaluations and nearest-neighbor prediction with the same examples. With four examples, MolReJev and a trained text baseline achieve similar ROC-AUC, with higher measured throughput for MolReJev. These results show that decision models can serve as in-context molecular predictors for compounds, drug pairs, and reactions.

papers.title: Learning Land-Surface Hydrology World Model from Satellite Observations
papers.summary: A world model should tell us not only what will happen, but what would happen under a different action. Learned Earth models now forecast remarkably well, yet forecast skill says little about what their state means or how it responds to a changed driver. We build LandWM, a world model of land-surface water in which rain is the action, learned from seven years of SMAP and CYGNSS observations: physical observation operators tie its latent state to soil water, and a mass-conserving balance governs how that state responds to rain. Over the U.S. Southern Great Plains, the model, never shown a soil-moisture value, tracks 28 in-situ probes as well as the operational SMAP Level-4 product, even from CYGNSS alone, and a storm added to the forcing of a station's cell wets its soil as natural storms wet the probes. Replace either piece and the forecasts stay, but the meaning goes: with neural operators, only a probe fitted to the stations finds the soil water; with a generic recurrent transition, rain on a single cell barely moves it. Yet when the same rain covers the whole region the two transitions swap roles, and the conserving one responds too weakly. Grounding makes a world model readable; its response to actions must be tested under more than one kind of intervention.

papers.title: STEdgeFormer: MCU and NPU Deployable Transformer Architecture
papers.summary: Transformer-based sequence models have achieved strong performance in language and time-series modeling, but self-attention remains computationally and memory intensive for deployment on resource-constrained edge accelerators. We propose STEdgeFormer, a lightweight, hardware-aware sequence architecture designed for efficient execution on embedded neural accelerators. STEdgeFormer combines polynomial mixture layers and DyT normalization with an accelerator-aware causal memory block, replacing pairwise self-attention with compact causal aggregation. On TinyStories, the fully NPU-supported STEdgeFormer (MW) achieves a perplexity of 7.39 with 4.12M parameters and 6.51 MB RAM, with an end-to-end latency of 40 ms. In comparison, the standard 4.12M-parameter configuration achieves a lower perplexity of 6.79 but requires CPU fallback for unsupported operators, resulting in 1450 ms latency. Vanilla Transformer, on the other hand, achieves a perplexity score of 5.71 using a 4.40M-parameter model, but it cannot be deployed on the hardware. On downstream tasks, STEdgeFormer achieves 94% accuracy on ECG5000 and 93% accuracy on Speech Commands with 1.39M parameters. These results demonstrate that hardware-aware architectural choices and operator compatibility can have a substantial impact on practical inference latency, beyond model size and task accuracy alone. Rather than targeting state-of-the-art accuracy on individual benchmarks, STEdgeFormer is designed to provide a deployable sequence modeling architecture under the memory, computational, and operator constraints of embedded neural accelerators.

papers.title: JAX-Nano: A GPU-Accelerated Differentiable Phonon Boltzmann Transport Solver for Nanoscale Heat Transfer
papers.summary: As semiconductor device dimensions approach phonon mean free paths, heat transport enters ballistic and quasi-ballistic regimes where Fourier's law becomes inadequate. The phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) describes these nonequilibrium effects but presents significant computational challenges. This work introduces JAX-Nano, a GPU-accelerated, end-to-end differentiable phonon BTE solver for nanoscale heat transport. The solver integrates steady-state and transient BTE formulations within a unified finite-volume framework, supporting structured and unstructured meshes, mode-resolved transport, phonon scattering, volumetric heat generation, and multiple boundary conditions. Automatic differentiation enables gradient computation with respect to transport properties, boundary conditions, heat-generation rates, and geometric parameters without separately derived adjoint equations. Numerical predictions are validated against analytical solutions and established BTE solvers across diffusive-to-ballistic regimes. Applications to complex three-dimensional geometries are demonstrated using single-fin, double-fin, and arrayed fin field-effect transistor (FinFET) configurations. Gradient-based inverse learning enables single- and multi-parameter identification, including simultaneous recovery of mode-resolved phonon relaxation times and spatially distributed heat-generation rates in steady-state and transient problems. GPU performance and scalability are evaluated with respect to spatial resolution, angular discretization, and phonon bands, including comparisons with an MPI-based BTE solver. JAX-Nano provides a unified computational framework for three-dimensional phonon transport, automatic differentiation, and inverse parameter identification, enabling sensitivity analysis and optimization of nanoscale thermal systems.

papers.title: FormaFin: Verifiable Financial Analysis with Solver-Guided Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Formally verifying financial analyses generated by large language models (LLMs) remains challenging as financial rules are largely expressed in natural language and rarely have corresponding formal specifications. Training language models to formalize these rules is hindered by the scarcity of labeled data and reliable training signals, while confidential financial data favor small models that run locally. We introduce FormaFin, a framework that trains small open language models to translate financial rules into reusable SMT formulas. FormaFin integrates teacher distillation with reinforcement learning using an SMT solver to compute rewards from numerical thresholds stated in financial rules. We evaluate FormaFin on corporate loan monitoring, in which lenders check borrowers' financial figures against loan agreements. To evaluate our framework, we curate \bench{}, a benchmark containing 143 loan agreements and 2,527 questions covering compliance, earnings cushion, and debt capacity. Our results show that a 7B formalizer achieves 94.8\% accuracy, outperforming open LLMs up to ten times larger. Across three model families, accuracy ranges from 92.6 to 96.8\%. Our framework also detects 95.6 to 99.7\% of errors in other LLMs' financial analyses. We make FormaFin and \bench{} publicly available.

papers.title: A Novel Approach to Clustering Shape Data Using Iteratively Weighted Vectors with k-Means
papers.summary: Topological data analysis provides a collection of methods for analyzing data with shape structure, including point clouds, graphs, and images. Recent advances in topological vectorization have enabled the embedding of shape data into Euclidean spaces, facilitating comparisons and machine learning tasks. Vector summaries that effectively capture topological structures are particularly useful for shape classification and unsupervised learning tasks such as clustering. We investigate the use of vectorized topological data for clustering through k-means, which partitions observations into a fixed number of groups by minimizing a squared-error loss function. By incorporating an element-wise weight-update step into the iterative k-means algorithm, we improve clustering performance on both simulated and real-world shape datasets. We show that estimating these weights reduces to a least-squares problem, requiring minimal additional computation while allowing flexible coefficient constraints. Our approach also substantially strengthens the negative correlation between the loss and clustering accuracy, improving the effectiveness of selecting among multiple clustering solutions based on the lowest loss. These improvements remain robust to changes in vector length and the number of initializations. Furthermore, weighted topological vector summaries exhibit stability under small structural perturbations, particularly when weight constraints are imposed. The proposed method offers a flexible alternative for clustering topological data, accommodating different k-means variants, vectorization methods, and weight constraints.

papers.title: Correlation-aware sequential sampling for multi-output polynomial chaos expansions
papers.summary: The interaction of multiple physical processes in complex engineering systems is often characterized by several quantities of interest (QoIs) with non-negligible cross-correlations. Accurate uncertainty quantification of these responses requires repeated model evaluations, which can be computationally expensive. As an alternative, polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) provides an efficient surrogate modeling framework for reducing this computational cost owing to its natural structure for statistical analysis, while adaptive sequential sampling can further improve sampling efficiency under a limited model evaluation budget. However, adaptive sampling strategies specifically designed for multi-output PCE remain limited, and existing approaches commonly aggregate information from individual outputs without explicitly accounting for their statistical dependence. When strong correlations exist among QoIs, output-wise aggregation can give greater combined influence to response patterns shared by several outputs. To reduce the influence of such repeated representation on sample allocation, this study develops a principal component analysis-based extension of the multi-output criterion for adaptive construction of PCE. The sampling criterion combines component-wise normalization with the retention of selected principal directions, thereby adjusting the relative influence of shared response patterns while preserving distance-based exploration. The method is verified through numerical examples with different levels of output coupling and is compared with the conventional multi-output criterion and reference sampling strategies. The results demonstrate that accounting for output dependence improves the allocation of new samples among multiple response features and enhances the efficiency of multi-output PCE surrogate construction, particularly for strongly correlated QoIs.

papers.title: Beyond Invoice Volumes: Temporal Network Structure, Maturity Concentration, and Systemic Liquidity Exposure in SME Trade-Credit Networks
papers.summary: Trade-credit invoices encode directed obligations whose temporal synchronization and counterparty concentration are obscured by annual volume totals. We audit 749,952 atomic B2B invoices from 2012-2023 (EUR 99.705B; 75,343 firms) from the pseudonymized Mendeley Data corpus (Esteva de la Rosa, 2026), separating 1,240 terminal 2024 bridge records (EUR 630.12M; 9 bridge-only firms) and 13 extreme-duration contracts (>3,650 days; EUR 297.75k). Using directed weighted graphs, HHI, Shannon entropy, CR1 shares, spectral centralities, and multi-cadence temporal operators, we formulate and benchmark a Maturity-Aware Network Exposure (MANE) indicator. Invoice values are heavily skewed: the top 1% hold 81.41% of value (Gini = 0.9742). Two-way fixed-effects panels with circular block bootstrapping ($B=999$, 12-month blocks) and Holm-Bonferroni control show higher lagged debtor counterparty concentration is associated with lower MANE ($\hatβ=-0.494$, 95% CI $[-0.752,-0.248]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.004$). Robustness audits (R1-R4) confirm stability under 2021 exclusion ($-0.402$, $p=0.004$), Shannon entropy ($+0.257$), CR1 ($-0.515$), 1%-99% Winsorization ($-0.462$, all $p=0.001$), and multi-invoice debtors (count $\ge 2$, $-0.334$, $p=0.031$). Conversely, within-FE diagnostics expose severe joint-concentration multicollinearity (VIF = 22.22) that vanishes for multi-invoice debtors ($p=0.719$), while regime splits reveal a macro reciprocity sign reversal between 2012-2019 ($-0.706$) and 2020-2023 ($+0.232$, both $p=0.001$). In 12-month purged forecasting, MANE does not reliably improve over maturity seeds ($Δ\mathrm{MSE}=2.668$, 95% CI $[-0.027,7.954]$; trimmed $0.067$, $[-0.035,0.194]$), positioning MANE as a reproducible screening and auditing diagnostic, rather than a default proxy, for supply-chain finance, multilateral clearing, and RWA tokenization.

papers.title: NAT: Scaling Causal Neural Action Tokenizers Across Embodiments
papers.summary: Action tokenizers let robot policies treat control as autoregressive next-token prediction. As these policies are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they will need a universal tokenizer that can encode actions from many embodiments and data sources, including ones it has not seen. We study action tokenization at scale, training on 49k hours of action data from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. We introduce Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a causal tokenizer whose decoder lets actions be executed as their tokens are generated. Across four simulation benchmarks, NAT outperforms FAST and prior neural action tokenizers when tokenizing unseen robot embodiments, and in vision-language-action models it outperforms FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot when acting through its tokens. NAT tokens also close the performance gap to a flow-matching action head on some benchmarks while lowering the inference latency for first actions. Our experiments also find that robot data may not be necessary to learn an effective action space: a NAT trained only on human hand motion performs close to tokenizers trained on robot data.

papers.title: Interaction Retention and Output-Likelihood Training in Parallel Sampling
papers.summary: Parallel samplers such as masked diffusion language models generate several coordinates per step from conditional marginals and randomize which coordinates are generated together, so even exact conditionals return a distorted distribution. We give an exact local account of this distortion. Around any full-support product law, the Gram operator of the sampler's response is diagonal in the interaction decomposition, and its eigenvalues are retention probabilities: the probability that an interaction has a unique latest-revealed coordinate. This retention spectrum determines the exact frontier between output accuracy and conditional calibration, its regularization path, and the population response of finite-mixture likelihood training. For pairwise interactions it yields a sharp dichotomy. Under homogeneous retention, output-likelihood training is equivalent to a single context gain; heterogeneous retention opens correction directions beyond any scalar, with an advantage bounded by an explicit heterogeneity gap. On binarized digits and MNIST, output-likelihood training within a heterogeneous schedule library lowers calibrated test negative log-likelihood in all twelve paired comparisons, and the gain survives pair-specific recalibration and a stronger path optimizer. For a frozen 169.6-million-parameter masked diffusion language model, serially normalized context gains are 1.070 and 1.056 at 8 and 16 rounds, against the predicted values 1.134 and 1.058.

papers.title: PhyMind: Physics-Informed Masked Autoencoding for EEG Foundation Models
papers.summary: EEG foundation models are pre-trained almost exclusively with masked reconstruction through a free-form decoder, sometimes with hand-crafted spectral targets added, as in MANAS-2. We study what happens when that decoder is replaced by a generative forward model of EEG. PhyMind keeps a standard masked transformer encoder, but its decoder must explain the masked signal through 68 cortical regions, each driven by damped stochastic oscillators and an aperiodic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, projected to the recording's own montage by a fixed boundary-element lead field evaluated per derivation. Training combines masked reconstruction with a Whittle spectral likelihood, an oscillator-dynamics residual, a minimum-norm source prior and a penalised neural residual. In a controlled comparison (same encoder, data, steps and seed), the physics decoder produces encoder tokens whose spectral content is far more linearly decodable than with a masked-autoencoder decoder or with the MANAS-2 objective: mean R^2 on a token-level spectral probe with amplitude-normalised targets is 0.67/0.77/0.77 on three datasets, against 0.24/0.50/0.50 (MAE) and 0.48/0.67/0.66 (MANAS-2 objective), approaching the released 92.8M-parameter MANAS-2 (0.71/0.81/0.80). Downstream gains in the controlled setting are small (four-task mean balanced accuracy 56.6 vs. 53.8 for MAE frozen, 63.8 vs. 62.7 fine-tuned). Region-level features from the physics decoder raise frozen four-class motor-imagery accuracy by 7-14 points, so a 7.2M-parameter model pre-trained on 3k hours of open EEG is comparable to the released MANAS-2 with frozen features (63.0 vs. 61.6). After full fine-tuning, MANAS-2 remains better (66.8 vs. 65.4 for our best model). The inferred sources do not reproduce the lateralisation that a classical inverse solution finds in motor imagery, so we do not claim anatomical interpretability. Code and weights are released.

papers.title: Dynamic Model Merging with Multi-Layer Aggregated Routing Evidence
papers.summary: Dynamic model merging aims to retain the efficiency of a unified model while better preserving task-specific expertise through input-dependent routing at both the task and head levels. However, even the routing components of the state-of-the-art approach remain limited: the task routing is highly sensitive to the choice of routing layer, whereas the head routing relies on simple max-logit competition. To address these limitations, we propose multi-layer aggregated routing evidence (MATE) as a unified mechanism for improving both task and head routing. Specifically, we first introduce a metric to quantify task routing separability across different layers. Empirical analysis of this metric reveals that different layers provide complementary evidence for identifying the tasks relevant to an input. Motivated by this observation, MATE selects multiple informative layers according to their routing separability and aggregates their layer-wise routing scores to produce a more robust signal that can be directly used for task selection. Moreover, we observe that this signal also encodes useful information about the suitability of the corresponding classification heads. This motivates us to further combine the MATE signal with the max-logit score to guide classification head selection. Extensive experiments on vision benchmarks demonstrate that MATE consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers.title: Twisted Block Particle Filters: A Local Particle-System Change of Measure for High-Dimensional State-Space Models
papers.summary: Block particle filters mitigate weight degeneracy in high-dimensional state-space models, but their normalizer estimates can remain highly variable. We introduce a twisted block particle filter (TBPF) that incorporates predictive guidance through an exact change of measure at blockwise resampling. The method guide-tilts one uniformly selected offspring per block, leaves the state-transition kernel unchanged, and computes the resampling correction using finite empirical guide averages. We prove that this correction exactly preserves the finite-particle block particle filter normalizer expectation, separating the effect of guided sampling from the approximation introduced by spatial blocking. Our analysis provides exact conditional local moments and a one-step conditional central limit result. We further derive explicit bounds on the correction accumulated across blocks and time, establish fixed-horizon consistency of the block filter and corrected normalizer under suitable regularity and guide-range conditions, and identify conditional criteria for guide perturbations that reduce variance. Experiments on coupled linear Gaussian and stochastic-volatility models with up to 256 latent dimensions show lower measured log-normalizer variance. For stochastic volatility with a five-step guide, the median reduction is $38\%$. An application to a 100-dimensional financial portfolio panel extends the evaluation to real data.

papers.title: AgriManager: A Framework and Benchmark for LLM-RL Generalization in Agricultural Management
papers.summary: Agricultural management is heterogeneous along two axes. The first is distributional shift within a fixed task interface: weather, crops, and prices vary across years and locations while sensors, actions, and objective stay fixed. The second is structural shift across interfaces: different farms expose different observed variables, available actions, and management objectives. We formalize the second axis as schema shift: variation in the policy-facing schema $Σ= (Σ_O, Σ_A, Σ_R)$ between training and deployment. We test whether LLM-RL generalizes across both axes with AgriManager, to our knowledge the first framework that trains LLM policies with RL across multiple process-based crop simulators, unifying DSSAT, WOFOST, and Cycles. We design a three-tier generalization ladder: Tier 1 within-schema distributional shift, Tier 2 single-axis schema shift along $Σ_O / Σ_A / Σ_R$, Tier 3 compositional schema shift across simulators, all scored on a frozen held-out test suite with three training seeds per method. Within fixed schemas, Qwen3-4B trained by RL with explicit reasoning exceeds neural-network PPO trained with the same interaction budget; without reasoning, training stalls near no-action where the reward penalizes input use. Under single-axis schema shift, $Σ_O$ transfer needs decision-critical state, $Σ_A$ results are consistent with joint action-menu coverage, and with reasoning a policy trained on yield alone transfers to unseen objectives. Under compositional schema shift, single-source training mostly hurts zero-shot transfer across simulators, and a unified policy trained only on other combinations of the same components recovers about 86% of the gain of a specialist trained on the target combination on DSSAT and stays below the specialists on the WOFOST and Cycles profit targets. Project page: https://agrimanager-framework.github.io

papers.title: Learning How a Body Moves: Few-Shot Body Inference for Visual World Models of Animated Characters
papers.summary: Two visually identical animated characters can respond differently to the same action command because their body dynamics differ. For example, a stiff blob and its bouncy twin reach different heights when both receive the jump command. Given only the first frame and the action command, a visual world model has no information to distinguish these twins, because their initial appearances are identical. We therefore propose an in-context world model that encodes clips of a character's other actions into a body representation, using a contrastive loss to separate look-alike characters. We introduce ToonTwins, a benchmark of 144 2D cartoon characters that run, jump, fall, turn and crouch. Its characters form look-alike groups of four that differ only in their dynamics profile, and we also evaluate the model on 32 animated animals from DeformingThings4D. Even with a body code from these clips, the latent pixel world model we tested recovered at most 25 percent of the twins' jump height difference. On new shapes, our model identified the correct twin in 85.9 percent of cases, compared with 76.7 percent for a transformer baseline that reads the same clips without a body summary, and in a controlled ablation the contrastive loss gave more than half of this gain. On the animated animals, it reduced the mean path prediction error by 8.5 percent against a model without body information.

papers.title: Task-Conditioned Detail Allocation for Synthetic Segmentation Data
papers.summary: Synthetic images sharing a segmentation label can differ in their training value. We propose Task-Conditioned Detail Allocation (TCDA) to select useful candidates and locally edit some remaining images. We ask whether image details provide class-specific cues in the regions marked by the label. We train a small task reference on frozen image features from real training images. We compare its class responses before and after blurring each candidate, and score how well these response changes align with the labeled regions. This detail allocation score ranks candidates from the same source. Comparing their response--label alignment with that of the real source image also guides repair decisions and, in multiclass tasks, the choice of regions to edit. Selected candidates and accepted repairs are used for training with the original labels and the unchanged downstream segmenter. Experiments on camouflaged object detection, degraded salient object detection, and adverse-condition semantic segmentation show that our selection outperforms equally sized random and label-agreement subsets. Combining selection and repair improves over real-only training by up to 0.019 in $S_α$ on COD10K and 2.86 mIoU points on ACDC.

papers.title: Hidden Sensitivity in LLM Pre-training: A Dynamic System View
papers.summary: In Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, loss curves can conceal substantial instability, i.e., even small perturbations may lead to dramatically different predictions while leaving loss nearly unchanged. To investigate this phenomenon and reveal the underlying mechanisms, we first formulate LLM pre-training as a non-autonomous dynamical system that jointly evolves model weights and Adam optimizer states. Based on this formulation, we introduce a normalized sensitivity score in optimizer-relative coordinates to identify sensitive training checkpoints. At one such checkpoint, a weight perturbation of only 10^(-5) leads to 35.7% disagreement in top-1 predictions and 16.2% disagreement in benchmark answers after 200 training steps, with only 0.8% of greedy generations remaining identical despite similar validation losses. Furthermore, we find that perturbations to Adam's first and second moments induce comparably large effects, with similar sensitivity patterns observed in OLMo-1B. Finally, guided by our diagnostic, targeted stabilization reduces top-1 disagreement to 0.83% and increases generation exact match to 88.3%, at the cost of a 0.11-nat increase in validation loss. Our findings reveal a hidden form of optimizer-state-dependent sensitivity in LLM pre-training that conventional loss-based evaluations may overlook, while demonstrating its potential for diagnosis and mitigation.

papers.title: More Is Never Less: Affordable Robustness to Additive Attacks via Monotone Multiple-Instance Learning
papers.summary: Static malware detectors that represent each sample as a bag of extracted features, such as permissions, API calls, or imported functions, are cheap to deploy and remain state-of-the-art under temporal drift and in selective classification. Yet, attackers can evade them by adding benign-looking content that outweighs malicious evidence. Canonically, detectors encode the presence of a few thousand features, selected during training, as sparse multi-hot vectors over a fixed vocabulary. Features that emerge after training remain invisible. We show that linear models and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) over this input are sum-pooled set models in disguise. Sum-pooling lets added benign features cancel malicious evidence. Instead, we cast malware detection with set-shaped static features as a multiple-instance learning (MIL) problem. To this end, we propose MalSets, which uses max-pooled Deep Sets models with a monotone head to ensure that any malicious evidence remains undiluted; thus, more is never less. Under MIL, a general text encoder maps any feature string to an embedding, thus eliminating the long-standing out-of-vocabulary problem at test time. Max-pooling retains the malicious evidence regardless of how many benign features an attacker adds. Since max-pooling can only grow when features are added, constraining the head alone makes the malware score monotone under additions, even against a white-box attacker adapted to this architecture. While monotone detectors are never evaded by state-of-the-art black-box or white-box attacks, they often significantly pay for this robustness in clean performance since benign features cannot count as evidence. However, by combining a non-monotone set encoder with max-pooling and a monotone head, MalSets maintains the robustness of prior monotone classifiers while achieving state-of-the-art performance.

papers.title: Statistical mechanics of linear classification on hierarchical tree data
papers.summary: Deep networks owe much of their success to their ability to exploit the structure in data, from the grammar of language to the multi-scale organization of images. Yet, many statistical mechanics approaches to structured data rely on Gaussian equivalence, whose assumptions can fail when a few latent variables influence all input coordinates. In this work, we take a step beyond this setting with a simple setup, in which a linear classifier is trained to infer the root of the classical broadcast process on a tree from its $N$ leaves. Despite this simplicity, the data already display non-Gaussian statistics along the direction carrying the label, as well as strong finite-size effects. By retaining the exact law along this direction and approximating the transverse fluctuations as Gaussian, we obtain a finite-depth replica theory that accurately describes the measured learning curves. At large depth and sufficiently weak regularization, we uncover a double descent whose two stages are separated in scale. In a range of broadcast noise below the reconstruction threshold, the first descent occurs at a number of samples scaling as $N^ω$, with $0<ω<1$ set by the data statistics, whereas the overfitting peak occurs at order $N$ samples. Beyond linear classifiers, this setup could serve as a controlled starting point to study deeper architectures and generative models on hierarchical data.

papers.title: Pixel Auto-Encoder: Reconstructing Language Model Activations Through Pixel Art
papers.summary: Interpreting the high-dimensional internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains a challenging problem. Recent approaches have explored translating these representations into human-understandable forms, particularly natural language. In this work, we explore the use of images as an alternative target modality for interpreting LLM activations. As a first step toward this goal, we introduce Pixel Auto-Encoder, which converts intermediate LLM activations into $32 \times 32$, 32-color pixel art and reconstructs them for subsequent computation within the model. By encouraging the intermediate representations to resemble predefined concept images, we investigate whether LLM activations can be expressed visually while preserving the model's language capabilities. We find that the model can produce target-aligned images for some concepts, and that replacing pixel representations with concept images can influence next-token predictions. However, we also observe a trade-off between visual alignment and language-model performance, as well as sensitivity to pixel-level changes that are difficult to interpret visually. These findings demonstrate the feasibility and limitations of image-based representations of LLM activations.

papers.title: Beyond Raw IQ: Compact Semantic Representations for Task Oriented Automatic Modulation Classification
papers.summary: Automatic modulation classification (AMC) is an important component of modern wireless communication systems, but conventional signal representations can be expensive to store, process, and communicate, particularly under noisy channel conditions. This work investigates whether learned semantic representations can provide a compact alternative to high-dimensional in-phase and quadrature (IQ) representations while retaining robustness to noise. Starting from a 2048-dimensional IQ representation, we evaluate learned semantic representations with dimensions of 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64. Across the evaluated configurations, a 16-dimensional representation provides the strongest overall trade-off between classification performance, robustness, and representation size. The resulting representation achieves a 128x compression ratio and a 99.22% reduction in dimensionality. We further evaluate representation stability across signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), compare semantic representations with a raw-IQ CNN, analyze per-class robustness, and perform five-seed validation. The five-seed evaluation produces an average accuracy of (49.22 +- 0.52)% and Macro-F1 of (49.27 +- 0.53)% across the evaluated SNR range. These results indicate that learned semantic compression can produce a substan- tially smaller representation while preserving useful classification information and improving geometric stability under noise.

papers.title: Learning free energy across a differentiable temperature range by deep generative modeling
papers.summary: Free energy governs the directionality, stability, and temperature sensitivity of physical, chemical, and biological transformations. Conventional free energy calculations, such as thermodynamic integration and free energy perturbation, often have to be performed at individual temperatures and are limited by the high cost of sampling an extensive set of thermodynamic states. Here, we introduce learned temperature-differentiable free energy perturbation (TD-FEP), a deep generative framework that learns a temperature-conditioned, invertible mapping between reference and target systems through data-free, energy-based optimization. TD-FEP thereby unifies one-shot state generation and free energy calculation across a continuous temperature range. We validated TD-FEP across a broad range of applications, including isolated molecules, periodic materials, and chemical reactions.

papers.title: RadAG: Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment of Diffusion Models
papers.summary: Diffusion and flow-based models have achieved remarkable success in generation, yet their samples often remain suboptimal in fidelity and text alignment. Two lines of inference-time methods address this: extrapolation guidance, such as classifier-free guidance (CFG) and its variants, and reward guidance, which aligns samples with reward models of human preference. Extrapolation guidance needs only forward passes, but it builds its reference by heuristic rules unrelated to the reward and therefore cannot steer sampling toward a given reward. Gradient-based reward guidance steers sampling directly toward a higher reward, but backpropagates through the entire generator at every step. This trade-off raises the question of whether extrapolation guidance can steer sampling toward a higher reward without a full backward pass. To answer this, we introduce Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance (RadAG), which constructs the reference by perturbing the attention logits of a single block against their reward gradient and extrapolates away from it. We prove that this update increases the reward of the clean estimate to first order, while its backward pass stops at the perturbed block instead of traversing the entire generator. On FLUX.2-klein-4B and 9B with PickScore and aesthetic rewards, RadAG achieves the highest target reward in every setting with 30-65% less time than gradient-based and candidate-based baselines.

papers.title: Synthetic EHR Generators Should Be Audited Like LLMs
papers.summary: Synthetic electronic health record (EHR) generation is increasingly adopting large autoregressive models, yet privacy evaluation has not kept pace, relying heavily on similarity-based heuristics and aggregate metrics that can obscure patient-specific memorisation. We argue that these models should additionally undergo LLM-style memorisation audits at the level of individual patient records. We support this position by comparing membership-inference evaluations across four prominent autoregressive EHR generators, highlighting inconsistent evaluation practices in patient representations and attack procedures. We evaluate trajectory reconstruction from partial context and introduce randomly assigned patient-level canaries to distinguish memorised associations from clinical generalisation. We examine these methods in a GPT-2-style model deliberately overfit to 1,000 MIMIC-IV patient trajectories, creating a controlled setting in which memorisation should be readily detectable. The model systematically recovers training patients' canaries, and their trajectory reconstruction approaches perfect accuracy with increasing context. Held-out patients show no systematic canary recovery, while reconstruction remains low and improves only marginally with additional context. These experiments establish a positive-control baseline for further evaluation of these methods in realistically trained models.

papers.title: ArrythML-II: An Optimized TinyML Framework for ECG Arrhythmia Detection and Multi-Class Beat Classification on Wearable Devices
papers.summary: This paper presents ArrythML-II, an optimized TinyML framework for on-device ECG arrhythmia detection and multi-class beat classification on wearable platforms. A systematic hyperparameter optimization framework is developed to identify compact autoencoder architectures for binary ECG arrhythmia detection. A custom scoring mechanism jointly considers detection performance, reconstruction-error thresholds, and model size to guide architecture selection. The framework is further extended to six-class ECG beat classification using a lightweight classifier derived from the optimized autoencoder architecture. Both models are INT8 quantized and deployed using TensorFlow Lite Micro on a custom-developed, battery-operated, single-lead ECG device based on the PSoC~6 microcontroller. The deployed autoencoder and classifier have model sizes of approximately 44~KB and 22~KB, respectively, with end-to-end processing times of 5.1~ms and 4.7~ms per ECG segment. Model inference accounts for 3.95~ms and 1.38~ms of these processing times, respectively. In the refined arrhythmia detection evaluation using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, the autoencoder achieved an accuracy of 84.76\%, precision of 82.68\%, and recall of 77.99\%. The multi-class classifier achieved 82.29\% accuracy, weighted precision of 90.18\%, and weighted recall of 82.29\%. Beyond offline model evaluation, the wearable platform is validated using preloaded ECG segments, live ECG signals, and an ESP32-S3-based ECG emulator that replays annotated MIT-BIH recordings as analog waveforms. The results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating optimized TinyML models into wearable platforms for real-time ECG analysis.

papers.title: Joint Client Scheduling and Resource Allocation for Optimal Federated Learning over Wireless Networks
papers.summary: Federated learning often relies on partial client participation because full participation is costly in cross-device wireless systems with limited uplink resources, heterogeneous channel conditions, energy constraints, and strict upload deadlines. However, partial participation introduces sampling variance, causing the sampled update to deviate from the full-participation update. Existing optimal client sampling methods reduce this variance but usually rely on simplified client-count budgets, while wireless-aware scheduling methods account for communication constraints but do not directly optimize sampling variance. This paper proposes resource-aware optimal client sampling (RAOCS), a unified variance-minimizing client scheduling framework under uplink resource-block, round deadline, update-information, and energy constraints. The resulting problem admits a capped water-filling solution that balances client update importance, wireless resource cost, and energy feasibility. Experimental results demonstrate that RAOCS achieves accuracy comparable to that of OCS while reducing the average upload time per iteration by more than a factor of 252.

papers.title: Multi-Order Passive Macromodeling from Layouts via Nested Port-Hamiltonian Learning
papers.summary: Compact, passive state-space macromodels of interconnects and power-delivery networks are essential for stable transient signal- and power-integrity simulations. However, conventional flows require costly per-layout full-wave electromagnetic (EM) simulations, while both traditional fitting and prior learning surrogates rely on post-hoc fitting or passivity perturbation that degrades accuracy without guaranteeing convergence. In this work, we propose an end-to-end macromodeling framework that learns directly in the passive space, mapping physical layout graphs to multi-order port-Hamiltonian (pH) macromodels. Specifically, our network encodes each layout graph into unconstrained matrix blocks and assembles them via a complete, prefix-nested pH parameterization that guarantees continuous-frequency passivity and stability by construction, yielding valid $k$-state macromodels via direct state slicing in one forward pass. To train all orders without reference realizations, we supervise the network directly on S-parameters through a progressive order-growth curriculum. Evaluated on 27k unseen test structures from a 270k-structure advanced-packaging dataset, our framework reduces mean S-parameter error by $42\%$ on average (up to $65\%$) over established macromodeling tools fitted to ground-truth EM responses, achieves zero passivity violations across $459{,}000$ exported models, and accelerates macromodel generation by $11{,}000$--$39{,}000\times$ ($36$--$85$~ms per layout).

papers.title: TesseraFlow: Scalable Video Diffusion for Dynamic Medical Imaging Inverse Problems
papers.summary: Generative priors are state-of-the-art for modeling medical images in image reconstruction tasks, but reconstruction with video priors takes tens of seconds to minutes per frame. Latent priors inherit the errors of their autoencoder, the memory of pixel-space whole-frame priors grows with the frame size, and pixel-space patch priors are slow for two reasons. First, their deep networks process every frame at full resolution at every sampling step, even though early steps resolve only low frequencies. Second, their samplers spend many network evaluations per sampling step on overlapping windows, multiple re-noising rounds, or backpropagation through the prior. We introduce TesseraFlow, a complex-valued pixel-space flow prior that reduces the first cost. A global encoder reads a low-resolution view of every frame once per sampling step. A single shallow decoder operates on this view during early steps and on full-resolution space-time tiles during later steps, so no network processes a whole frame at full resolution. Our sampler, ReTile, addresses the second reason. We use randomized grid shifting at every sampling step along with re-noising, which acts as a stochastic gradient instead of computing overlapping tiles, so a single network pass per sampling step suffices. On its own, ReTile speeds up an existing global-context patch prior by 6-9x, and our prior adds a further 3-5x speedup. TesseraFlow reconstructs about one 256x256 frame per second, 20-367x faster than patch and latent video priors, and can match or exceed the best generative baseline on cardiac, brain, and abdominal MRI and lung CT, at a fraction of its GPU time.

papers.title: JEPA-Tuner: From Predictive Fine-Tuning to Asynchronous Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate sequences of actions from visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions. In embodied interaction, executing these actions influences subsequent observations and robot states, providing a natural predictive signal for policy learning. However, standard action-supervised fine-tuning does not explicitly capture these action-conditioned temporal dependencies in the guidance consumed by the action predictor. We introduce JEPA-Tuner, a predictive fine-tuning framework that regularizes the VLA's native policy guidance through action-conditioned future prediction. During fine-tuning, a predictor in JEPA-Tuner learns to match guidance encoded from a future observation given the current guidance and committed actions. This objective encourages a cross-modal guidance adapter to capture how the scene and robot state evolve under those actions, while jointly training the action expert on both observed and predicted guidance keeps the representation informative for control. In addition, when deploying the VLA model with asynchronous action-chunk inference, the pre-trained predictor will anticipate the guidance needed at the next chunk boundary. The policy can thus generate the next chunk in advance and execute it from its first action without overlap correction or additional predictor training, enabling efficient and high-quality asynchronous execution. Experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World show that JEPA-Tuner improves task success under synchronous inference with better multi-modal guidance embeddings. For asynchronous control, JEPA-Tuner improves performance and smoothness across different latency settings on both LIBERO simulator and multi-size real robot demonstrations. The project website with video demos is at https://qujx.github.io/JEPA-Tuner-Website.

papers.title: Do LLM Agents Compromise Like Humans? Risk and Responsibility in Dyadic Decision-Making
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they must collaborate to make joint decisions. We investigate how this collaboration unfolds under risk, asking whether agents adjust their choices to accommodate their partners, how they assign responsibility for shared outcomes, and whether responsibility attribution shapes subsequent adjustment. We designed a series of agents with systematically varying risk preferences and paired them in a repeated joint decision-making task previously conducted with humans. Like humans, agents converged toward their partners' choices. However, similar aggregate behavior arose from different dynamics: agents showed little evidence of reciprocal adjustment, tended to weigh rewards more, and their responsibility attribution was decoupled from compromise. Similarly, while they showed bias in their responsibility attribution, the outcome's valence shaped the attribution differently than in humans. Our results reveal important differences between human--human and agent--agent joint decision-making, demonstrating that similar social outcomes can emerge from different social dynamics and reasoning.

papers.title: Do You Even Know What I Want? Improving LLMs Ability to Detect Hidden User Intent
papers.summary: As with conventional AI agents, a common source of misalignment between Large Language Models (LLMs) and their human users is misspecified goals. Often, this happens when the human has skewed beliefs about the system's model and provides it with information that causes behavior different from what they expected, with potentially unwanted side effects. To ensure goal alignment, one solution would be for the LLM to ask the human questions about their objectives. However, it has been well-documented that LLMs most often provide default responses to user requests rather than try and ask questions to clarify their true intent. In this paper, we address these challenges by adapting a novel formulation for the objective misspecification problem to work with LLMs. We then test if LLMs that are prompted to ask questions about a user's true underlying objectives are better at identifying them compared to those that do not. We evaluate our method using four state-of-the-art LLMs tested on five standard IPC domains, showing that for some domains, asking questions greatly improved model performance.

papers.title: Watermark Claims Under Test: Lessons from Auditing a Production LLM
papers.summary: Can we tell whether an LLM is watermarked without knowing its secret key? Published black-box tests suggest that carefully designed prompts can reveal the statistical footprint of a watermark. This paper examines what happens when those tests move from controlled reference implementations to a deployed model whose watermarking parameters are undisclosed. We present an audit of the Red-Green watermark presence test on Claude. Across ten initial configurations, the published test never rejects on a model the provider states is watermarked, despite detecting a local reference at comparable sample sizes. Controlled experiments expose a failure mode: including the prompt in the watermark's repeated-context history suppresses marking exactly where the test measures it. The watermark remains active, but the probe becomes blind. Attempts to repair the probe reveal further confounds. Constructed contexts can trigger native digit-to-word preferences, while comparisons within a single response can measure how the model plans its answer. Tokenization changes which contexts the probe actually controls. These findings show why validation on a surrogate model does not establish validity on the model under investigation. A redesigned probe finds a substantial context-dependent shift on Claude Fable that is absent on two sibling controls. However, the pre-registered decision remains inconclusive because selective refusals violate the protocol, and the effect's watermark origin is unresolved. We show how to design controls, distinguish statistical rejection from evidence of watermarking and interpret a null without treating it as proof of absence. We provide researchers and practitioners working on LLM evaluation, watermarking, and provenance with an audit checklist grounded in concrete successes and failures. Code, prompts, and parsed responses are available for reproducing the analyses.

papers.title: Consumer-Time Validity in Stateful AI Runtimes: Verifying Recovered State and Deferred Authority
papers.summary: Stateful LLM serving engines and agent runtimes reuse execution state and deferred permissions across components and sessions. A cancellation, rollback, or approval is recorded by one component and relied on by another, and recording it does not make the later use valid: a downstream consumer may read state or dispatch an action whose identity, production status, allocation, or target revision has since changed. We call the missing check consumer-time validity and separate two forms. State validity governs what a consumer reads. On vLLM with LMCache, an interrupted KV load leaves unwritten blocks indexed, and a host-only counter rewind desynchronizes the GPU position, so a second tenant generates a schema-valid tool call naming the wrong tenant in 10/10 native-fault runs; the call is recorded and not executed. Authority freshness governs what a consumer executes: on a multi-session approval runtime, an unrevoked deferred grant overwrote a newer revision in one admitted live execution. Output equality cannot test state validity: a fault-free run diverges at token 30 through BF16 batching alone while attended-KV digests match. We therefore specify consumer-bound recovery contracts that, for state recovery, jointly require exclusion, retention, and task completion, and an admissible-witness standard realized as a GPU-free offline trace verifier over scheduler metadata and persisted tool artifacts. On recorded traces the verifier agrees with the reference verdicts in 42/42 frozen GPU-matrix scenarios. An allocation-aware repair satisfies 7/7 triggered vLLM fault predicates on a pinned scheduler-case matrix, where upstream PR 61769 satisfies 2/7, and revision-bound dispatch blocks all 160 deterministic conflicting overwrites in a separate dispatcher cohort. Recovery must be checked where state and authority are consumed, with evidence bound to the consuming request.

papers.title: World Models for Ocean Engineering: A Critical Review of Maritime Autonomy, Adaptive Latent Prediction, Digital Twins, and Biodiversity Monitoring
papers.summary: Marine robots face partial observability, non-stationary dynamics, and sparse communication, motivating WMs that learn compact predictive states for planning. This review develops a functional taxonomy of WMs for ocean engineering, focusing on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) and AdaJEPA's test-time adaptation within model predictive control, mapping them to navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring, and separating demonstrated evidence from prospective applications. The synthesis identifies key Gaps: benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, safe adaptation and proposes a research agenda for physics-informed, deployment-adaptive marine WMs validated through simulation and field missions.

papers.title: A Design Space for Data Agents: Insights from KDD Cup 2026
papers.summary: Data agents interpret analytical requests, gather evidence from heterogeneous sources, and compute results within finite resource budgets. We analyze the final code submissions of the ten highest-ranked teams in the KDD Cup 2026 Data Agents for Complex Data Analysis competition. We organize the observed design choices into three interacting layers, covering workflow orchestration, analytical functions, and working state. The comparison reveals recurring patterns for allocating computation in response to task progress, structuring evidence for computation and assessment, and preserving reusable artifacts with their provenance. Candidates that rely on the same evidence can inherit the same error, so interpreting their agreement requires tracing those dependencies. The design space motivates controlled evaluations of how resource allocation, evidence sharing, and targeted recovery affect task completion and correctness.

papers.title: Who Gets Re-ranked When a Clinical Model Gains New Data?
papers.summary: Hospitals often update a deployed risk model by adding a data source, such as laboratory results, that only some patients have. Work on safe model updates assumes fixed inputs and so ignores patients who lack the new data. The update has no new measurements for them, yet their rank can change, and a sick patient not yet tested can drop off an alert list. We split rank-based compatibility by data availability and pair it with error correction and alert-list effects. We compared each update with ordinary retraining on the old inputs, predicting ICU admission or death and hospital admission, on 78,475 emergency department visits from MC-MED and, in a pre-registered replication, 100,000 stays from MIMIC-IV-ED at a second hospital. Radiograph report text gave no detectable gain and almost no extra re-ranking. Laboratory results improved prediction but, at both hospitals and with linear or tree models, pushed patients without labs down alert lists; linear updates also reshuffled them more than retraining did, without ranking them better. A top-20% admission list caught 4.2% of admitted patients without labs after the update, against 18.8% after retraining (second hospital: 4.9% against 22.6%), while catching more patients overall. This held for list sizes from 5% to 50% and in every patient group we checked, despite better measured calibration. Separate alert thresholds for patients with and without labs restored most or all of their catch rate at both hospitals at almost no cost. Teams should check these patients before deploying such an update.

papers.title: PruneNAS: Constraint Aware Neural Architecture Search based Pruning
papers.summary: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has achieved state-of-the-art performance across diverse tasks, but its high computational cost remains a major barrier. We introduce PruneNAS, a novel framework that integrates structured pruning into NAS to efficiently explore high-performing architectures while leveraging pretrained models. Unlike conventional NAS methods that train each candidate from scratch, PruneNAS generates a candidate pool by pruning pretrained networks at multiple granularity levels and formulates the selection as a global optimization problem using training-free importance metrics. This approach enables rapid evaluation of candidate architectures under strict resource constraints, dramatically reducing search time from hundreds of GPU hours to mere minutes. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that PruneNAS discovers compact, high-accuracy architectures that nearly halve the computational cost (MACs) of prior methods on ResNet-50, while also showing strong generalization on object detection tasks with YOLO. Our method bridges structured pruning and NAS, offering a practical solution for resource-constrained model deployment.

papers.title: Micro Operational Robustness of LLMs on Code Generation
papers.summary: It is now common practice in software development for large language models (LLMs) to be used to generate program code. It is desirable to evaluate the robustness of LLMs for this usage. This paper is concerned in particular with how sensitive LLMs are to variations in descriptions of the coding tasks. However, existing techniques for evaluating this robustness are unsuitable for code generation because the input data space of natural language (NL) descriptions is discrete and sparse. To address this problem, we propose a robustness evaluation method called scenario domain analysis, which aims to find the expected minimal change in the NL descriptions of coding tasks that would cause the LLMs to produce incorrect outputs. We have formally proved the theoretical properties of the method and also conducted extensive experiments to evaluate the robustness of four state-of-the-art LLMs: Gemini-pro, Codex, Llamma2 and Falcon 7B, and have found that we are able to rank these with confidence from best to worst. Moreover, we have also studied how robustness varies in different scenarios, including the variations with the topic of the coding task and with the complexity of its sample solution, and found that robustness is lower for more complex tasks and also lower for more advanced topics, such as multi-threading and data structures.

papers.title: OmniDecisionBench: Evaluating and Benchmarking the Multimodal Jev-Style System One Decision Models
papers.summary: Multimodal System One models answer visual tasks with typed decisions and native probabilities, yet no holistic evaluation compares them with general VLMs or maps either class's capability boundaries. We introduce OmniDecisionBench, a holistic benchmark of multimodal System One models. Its main evaluation assigns 45 datasets (192,975 records) to five capability families and twelve primary angles across four typed interfaces, scoring accuracy and candidate-probability calibration. A validation layer adds three single-factor diagnostics varying visual presentation, textual evidence sufficiency, and target dataset. Across three System One models and two general VLMs, three regularities emerge. First, strengths depend on angle and metric: System One models lead discrete tasks overall with lower ECE15 on most perception, reading, and reasoning angles (Jev 1.14: 80.14% accuracy, 4.50% ECE15), while general VLMs lead ordinal grading and outperform Jev 1.14 among the three models tested on direct Box grounding. Second, multi-image and abstract reasoning bound every model, where confidence rather than accuracy separates them. Third, reliability shifts with the input: rendering only options nearly triples Jev 1.14's selective risk at nearly flat mean signed bias, and donor risk cutoffs often exceed target risk across unseen datasets and task families.
